In 1983, the American video game industry crashed, ultimately creating a void filled by Nintendo and Sega, who proceeded to release their game consoles with top-notch games. It wasn't until the 16-bit era that PC and console games began to surpass arcade games in quality, leading to the slow death of arcade gaming.

  • What would it take for me to go back to an arcade? I'd say that there needs to be a good variety of games (old game cabinets along with some rare niche games you won't find anywhere else). If there's an arcade with the same old standbys such as Tekken and Time Crisis 3, I wouldn't care.

  • There is really nothing arcades could do to be financially successful. Arcade gaming has been dead since the late-90s/early-2000s. While there still are arcades these days, many of them are enormous Dave-and-Busters that are located in premium suburban malls in big cities. Most of the other arcades are small corners found in hotels and movie theaters that have a Time Crisis, House of the Dead and a crane machine. There are "barcades" in college towns, which are hipster bars with craft beers and some old cabinets such as Space Invaders and Pac Man. However, the "barcade" seems to be a fad on the decline, with some of them closing down in the past few years.

It depends on the type of vibe you're going for. If your opening an arcade bar, you don't want a DDR machine... Especially when you can get 4 cabinet classics for the same price. The trick with the fancy brand new machines is that they are expensive as hell. 20k, sometimes more. And with an overhead that high, your stick charging $1 a play, or leasing the machine, or both.

I'm personally of the opinion that cheaper games = more repeat business. Make your money up on drinks, or snacks, but keep your hands at 25 or 50c a play. But if you're going for kid friendly, you have a bigger challenge. The new cabinets are expensive (and can mostly be played in iPhone), and kids won't have the nostalgia for older games.

So, assuming you are going for the 21+ crowd:

Skip redemption (ticket games). Unless you can afford to buy prizes in bulk, it's not worth it. The games take up a ton of floorspace, are expensive to repair, and mostly suck anyway.

Get educated. Learn how the machines work, at the very least the coin slots, so you can make repairs yourself. This will reduce your overhead.

Curate your selection: pick games you would want to play, as well as ones with mass appeal. Older games will be cheaper, and you'll get me bang for your buck, but one or two popular modern flagship games might do you well.

Be artistic. Or pay someone else to be. The decor and music of your place is as important as your game selection. Your going for a 'cool place to hang out' vibe... Nothing kills that like bare white drywall.

Fuck Golden Tee. People can go to the sports bro bar for that, and they will. Don't bother trying to attract a market that is already being served.

Either stay cheap and accessible, or be prepared to go fit the "premium" route. There are places here in Chicago that have free games, and expensive drinks, and they pack people in on Friday, because it's different and a little hip. They also don't open the full bar outside of weekend, leaving 60% of their space blocked off during the week. The more casual place, with cheaper beer and quarter games? 7 days a week.

Anyway, those are my observations, and done food for thought. Good luck.
